rationale: While Karayol et al. (2024) report a cohort of 25 individuals with de novo MSL2 variants and qualitatively list vision problems among secondary features observed 'to a lesser extent' (alongside seizures, sleep disturbance, and connective tissue signs), the specific quantitative range of 25% to 45% (6/25 to 11/25) cannot be verified from the provided source text. Furthermore, pediatric ophthalmic literature indicates that refractive errors and strabismus occur at baseline frequencies of 25% to 44% in clinic-referred pediatric populations and non-specific developmental cohorts, which conflicts with using non-specific vision problems as a reliable discriminating feature against other chromatinopathies without detailed structural eye phenotyping.

evidence.text: In a cohort of 25 individuals with de novo heterozygous MSL2 variants, global developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, and motor coordination problems were core features, while vision problems, seizures, connective tissue disease signs, sleep disturbance, and other organ anomalies were reported 'to a lesser extent'.

Refractive errors and strabismus are highly prevalent in general pediatric and neurodevelopmental populations (25% to 45%), making non-specific visual problems non-discriminating unless defined by specific structural pathologies (e.g., coloboma, aniridia, or lacrimal duct anomalies).

new_directions.question_text: Do individuals with MSL2 syndrome systematically lack major structural anterior/posterior segment malformations (e.g., coloboma, optic nerve hypoplasia) compared to Wiedemann-Steiner or Rubinstein-Taybi syndromes?
new_directions.rationale: A negative predictive marker (absence of structural ocular malformations) provides much stronger differential diagnostic power than generic refractive errors.
